summary: Describes an experimental use of STUN that lets a client find out how the NATs and firewalls between it and a STUN server behave. This helps applications understand the kind of address translation and filtering they face. It was published as an experiment, not as a standard.

eli5.summary: You toss a few test balls through a gate to a friend and see which ones get through and which get blocked, to learn how the gate works.

questions: how to discover nat behavior with stun
what is stun nat behavior discovery
how to detect nat mapping and filtering type
what is the stun other-address attribute
how to measure nat binding lifetime
subtitle: A STUN usage that lets a client probe how the NATs and firewalls in front of it currently map and filter traffic.

tldr.problem: Applications behind NATs and firewalls often fail in the field in ways they did not in the lab, and they cannot tell how the NAT in the path is treating their traffic.
tldr.mechanism: The client sends STUN Binding Requests to a server with two IP addresses and two ports. New attributes (CHANGE-REQUEST, OTHER-ADDRESS, RESPONSE-PORT, RESPONSE-ORIGIN, PADDING) let it test mapping, filtering, binding lifetime, hairpinning and fragment handling.
tldr.outcome: Results show only the NAT's behavior at that instant, so applications must keep a reliable fallback. The RFC is Experimental, and it is updated by RFC 8553.

facts.label: Client rate limit
facts.value: No more than ten new transactions per second

facts.label: Tests per mapping or filtering check

today: RFC 5780 is an Experimental RFC, not a standard, and it is updated by RFC 8553. The text itself says the experiment was meant to show whether behavior discovery improves real applications.

sections.title: What the Experiment Is For
sections.content:
RFC 5780 defines an experimental STUN usage that discovers the presence and current behavior of NATs and firewalls between a STUN client and a STUN server. STUN itself (RFC 5389) lets a client learn its reflexive transport address with a Binding Request. This usage adds new attributes to the Binding Request and Binding Response so the client can probe the NAT.

The RFC is frank about the limits. NAT devices do not behave consistently, may become more restrictive under load, and can shorten binding lifetimes. Applications can discover how bad things currently are, but not how bad they will get. So the usage is meant for diagnostics and for tuning an application at run time, and applications that need reliable reach must use another technique such as ICE (RFC 5245) or RFC 5626.

It is Experimental because the authors want evidence that using the results as an optimization, with a reliable fallback, actually improves applications. A peer-to-peer overlay that chooses which nodes act as supernodes is the main example given.
sections.eli5: It is a way to peek at what the gate in front of your house is doing right now. The gate can change its mind, so you should always have a back door ready.

sections.title: The Tests It Enables
sections.content:
Mapping and filtering are described using the terms of RFC 4787: Endpoint-Independent, Address-Dependent, and Address and Port-Dependent. The overview lists what a client can check:

  • Mapping: does the NAT give the same public address and port no matter where the client sends to? It works for UDP, TCP or TCP/TLS.
  • Filtering: which sources can send back through the NAT? This applies only to UDP.
  • Binding lifetime: how long an idle NAT binding stays open, which tells the client how often to send keepalives. UDP only.
  • Hairpinning: the client sends a request to its own mapped address from another port and sees if it receives it.
  • Fragment handling: the PADDING attribute makes a message big enough to be fragmented. UDP only.
  • Generic ALG detection: the server returns both MAPPED-ADDRESS and XOR-MAPPED-ADDRESS, and if they differ, a NAT with a generic application level gateway is in the path.
sections.eli5: Each test is a different question to the gate: do you give me the same door number every time, who are you willing to let in, and how long do you remember me when I am quiet?

sections.title: Running the Mapping and Filtering Tests
sections.content:
Test I is a plain Binding Request. The server's reply carries OTHER-ADDRESS, its alternate IP address and port; if that is missing the server does not support the usage. If the mapped address equals the local socket address, the client is not NATed.

Mapping takes at most three tests. Test II sends to the alternate address with the primary port: if the mapped address matches test I, the NAT has Endpoint-Independent Mapping. Otherwise test III sends to the alternate address and port. A match with test II means Address-Dependent Mapping, and no match means Address and Port-Dependent Mapping.

Filtering also takes at most three tests and is sensitive to earlier traffic. Test II sets CHANGE-REQUEST to change both IP and port, so the response comes from a source the client never contacted. If it arrives, the NAT has Endpoint-Independent Filtering. If not, test III changes only the port: a response means Address-Dependent Filtering, and silence means Address and Port-Dependent Filtering.

Binding lifetime uses two source ports, X and Y. The client sends from X, waits T seconds, then sends from Y with RESPONSE-PORT pointing at X's mapped port. If the response shows up on X, the binding is still alive. Repeating with different T, as a binary search, finds the lifetime.

Tests should use a source port with no recent traffic, for example one held unused for at least 15 minutes, or a random port from the 32768-49151 or 49152-65535 ranges.
sections.eli5: To see who the gate lets in, ask a friend to answer from a different house number and then from a different door. Whether the answers get through shows how picky the gate is.

sections.title: The New STUN Attributes
sections.content:
All new attributes are used only in Binding Requests and Binding Responses. CHANGE-REQUEST existed in RFC 3489 and is redefined here.

  • CHANGE-REQUEST is a 32-bit attribute with two flags, A (change IP) and B (change port). It is allowed only in requests.
  • RESPONSE-ORIGIN tells the client the source address and port the response came from, which helps detect double NAT.
  • OTHER-ADDRESS gives the address and port the server would use if both change flags were set. It reuses the attribute number of the old CHANGED-ADDRESS and must not appear unless the server has a second IP address.
  • RESPONSE-PORT asks the server to send the response to a given port on the same IP address. Server support is optional.
  • PADDING is free-form filler used to force fragmentation. It should equal the outgoing interface MTU, rounded up to a multiple of four bytes.

A request that contains both RESPONSE-PORT and PADDING must be rejected with a 400 error.
sections.eli5: These are extra notes on the question: send your answer from the other door, tell me which door you really used, and stuff the envelope so thick it must be torn into pieces.

sections.title: Client and Server Behavior
sections.content:
A server should be configured with two separate public IP addresses and allocate the same pair of ports on both for each of UDP, TCP and TCP/TLS. If it cannot, it must not send OTHER-ADDRESS and must answer any request with CHANGE-REQUEST with a 420 error. A server with only one IP address must not be advertised with the SRV service names. The response always includes both MAPPED-ADDRESS and XOR-MAPPED-ADDRESS, plus RESPONSE-ORIGIN.

The source address and port of a response follow the CHANGE-REQUEST flags: with neither flag it uses the address and port the request arrived on, change IP swaps only the address, change port swaps only the port, and both flags swap both.

Clients should not start more than ten new STUN transactions per second. They should be ready for a 420 error on RESPONSE-PORT and on CHANGE-REQUEST when no OTHER-ADDRESS was received. Servers are found with SRV records using the service name stun-behavior for UDP and TCP, and stun-behaviors for TLS over TCP. By default the usage runs on the STUN ports, 3478 for UDP and TCP and 5349 for TCP over TLS.
sections.eli5: The helper needs two front doors and two windows so it can answer from a different place. The asker must not shout questions too fast.

sections.title: Security and IAB Considerations
sections.content:
The usage inherits the security considerations of STUN. OTHER-ADDRESS opens no new attacks, but an attacker who can alter the Binding Response can hide the STUN server from the client. Rejecting requests with both RESPONSE-PORT and PADDING prevents an amplification attack aimed at the originating address, and servers ignore padding longer than 64K. Servers may require authentication, and a 401 response means the client must get credentials or report a permanent failure.

Because this is a form of Unilateral Self-Address Fixing (UNSAF), the RFC includes the IAB considerations from RFC 3424: the problem definition, an exit strategy, the brittleness it may add, requirements for a long-term solution, and issues with existing NAPT boxes. On the exit strategy, it says the specification will be of no interest for v6-to-v6 connectivity.
sections.eli5: A sneaky person could pretend to be the helper, so the rules block tricks that would make the helper shout at someone else.
